en.title: Simple Guide to Registering in the Taxpayers' System for Small Businesses
en.description: A practical, step-by-step guide to registering in the Taxpayers' System designed specifically for small and medium-sized businesses, including useful tips and solutions to common problems.
en.body_html:
The Taxpayers' System (Samaneh-ye Moadian) is one of the most significant transformations in Iran's tax system in recent years. This system was designed to reduce paperwork, increase transparency, and streamline tax processes, and now almost all businesses are required to register in it. For owners of small businesses, who typically have limited time and resources, registering in this system can sometimes seem daunting. However, the reality is that with a little proper guidance, the process is entirely manageable.

In this article, we explain the registration steps for small businesses in a practical way without unnecessary complications. Our goal is that after reading this text, you can enter the system with complete confidence and register your information.

What is the Taxpayers' System and why is it important for your small business?

The Taxpayers' System is a platform through which the Iranian National Tax Administration communicates with taxpayers. In this system, electronic invoices are issued, purchases and sales are recorded, and tax returns are processed in a smarter and faster manner.

For small businesses, being present in this system means greater transparency in compliance with the law and, consequently, a reduced likelihood of fines and future disputes. In addition, many new tax facilities and exemptions can only be obtained through this system. Therefore, timely registration is not only a legal requirement but also an opportunity to better manage your business's taxes.

Preparing documents before starting registration

Before entering the system, it is better to prepare a few documents and pieces of information so that the process proceeds without interruption. You will typically need the business owner's identity information, a valid phone number and email, the exact postal code of the business location, details of the bank account related to economic activities, and, if applicable, business licenses or establishment permits.

If your business is a legal entity, company documents including the articles of association, latest registration changes, and introduction of a representative will also be required. We recommend saving all this information in an organized file so it is easily accessible when needed.

Registering on the Tax Administration's e-services portal (my.tax.gov.ir)

Registration starts on the Iranian National Tax Administration's own e-services portal, my.tax.gov.ir, not on a general government portal. If you have already registered there (for example for a tax return or an economic code), log in with that account.

If you do not have an account, register with your national ID number, date of birth and mobile number. The mobile number must be registered in your own name (or the company's legal representative), because the one-time password is sent to it. Later logins use your national ID, a password you set yourself, and an SMS code.

Steps to register in the Taxpayers' System

After logging in to my.tax.gov.ir, first complete your tax file registration if you do not yet have a tax file and economic code. Then use "Enter dashboard" to open your Taxpayers' System dashboard (tp.tax.gov.ir) and select the tax file you want to activate.

At this stage, carefully enter the identity information, address, type of economic activity, start date of operations, and other requested details. For small businesses, simpler options are usually displayed based on your scale of operations.

After completing the information, the system will review your request. This process may take a few minutes to a few hours. During this time, it is best to keep the page open or check your email.

Common problems and practical solutions

Many small businesses encounter issues during identity verification or document upload. If the system displays an "incomplete information" error, double-check all fields. Sometimes an extra space or typo can cause this error.

If the verification code is not sent, recheck the mobile number or use the resend option. In special cases where the system does not allow registration, the best solution is to contact the Taxpayers' System support or visit the nearest tax office.

Businesses that were previously registered in older systems may have their previous information transferred automatically. In this case, you only need to verify and update the information.

What to do after registration?

To issue invoices, obtain a unique tax memory ID (shenaseh-ye yekta-ye hafezeh-ye maliati) under "Tax file and membership" in your dashboard. While doing so you must choose how invoices will be sent: directly (you or your software sign and send them with your own private key), through a trusted tax service provider (with the provider's key or your own), or through government systems. Only one sending method can be active per unique ID at a time. Keep your password and private key safe.

Warning: there are no "test invoices" in the live dashboard. Every invoice you issue and register is real and affects your tax position and the buyer's. To practise, use your software's or trusted provider's sandbox, or issue your first real invoices carefully with an adviser. Many accounting programs are connected to the Taxpayers' System and can make the work easier.

Conclusion

Registration in the Taxpayers' System is no longer an option for small businesses but a necessity. With a little initial preparation and following the steps in order, this task can be completed easily and will help improve transparency and better tax management for your business in the long term.

If you encounter any doubts at any stage or the system behaves unexpectedly, seek guidance from reputable tax consultants or refer directly to the official website of the Iranian National Tax Administration. Starting on time and correctly will protect you from many future problems and penalties.

en.title: Tax Assessment Notice Has Arrived; What Should You Do Before Taking Any Action?
en.description: Check the deadline, compare the amount with your own records, and create a clear picture of the document before filing an objection or reaching an agreement.
en.body_html:
Receiving a tax assessment notice feels like an alarm bell for many taxpayers. The first reaction is sometimes anger and sometimes denial. Neither on its own will move the case forward. Before signing anything, making any rushed calls, or drafting any objection text, there are several calm steps you need to take.

First, read the notice in full. Note down the type of tax, the fiscal year, the declared income or tax base, the tax amount, and the date of service. The deadline runs from this date: under Article 238 of the Direct Taxes Act you have 30 days from the date of service to go to the tax office with your evidence or file a written objection. If you do nothing within those 30 days, the assessment becomes final and your options narrow sharply.

Second, place the authority’s figure next to your own. Ask whether the difference stems from sales, disallowed expenses, overlooked exemptions, or external indicators. Until the root of the discrepancy is clear, neither an agreement nor an effective brief is wise. A simple two-column table is enough: what you know versus what the notice states.

Third, gather documents, not emotions. Sales invoices, related bank statements, contracts, payroll lists, and Taxpayers' System (Samaneh-ye Moadian) reports are far stronger at this stage than any verbal explanation. Also list any missing documents; their absence itself forms part of the picture.

Fourth, understand your options. Sometimes a discussion to settle the matter under Article 238 is possible. In other cases, preparing a brief and appearing before the board is more appropriate. The choice depends on the strength of your documentation, the size of the difference, and your readiness for the timeline. Never choose a path simply because it “seems faster.”

Fifth, keep the language of your brief simple and well-documented. The board pays less attention to lengthy narratives than to orderly supporting evidence. Every claim should have an attachment. If you cannot prove a point, do not state it with certainty.

Sixth, consider the side effects. An agreement or ruling may affect other periods, value-added tax, or penalties. A long-term view means not closing this year’s case in a way that forces you to provide contradictory explanations next year.

Seventh, do not decide alone if the case is complex. A reliable advisor at this stage is someone who can read the notice in plain language for you and tell you which parts are genuinely defensible. There is no place here for promises of a guaranteed outcome; what can be provided is a clear picture of your options.

A tax assessment notice is not the end of the matter. It is the beginning of a documented dialogue. If you organize the deadline, the source of the dispute, and your documents in the first few days, the rest of the process will proceed more smoothly.

en.title: Mistakes That Make a Tax Return Fragile
en.description: Last-minute rush, inconsistent reports, and undocumented expenses make the file more vulnerable than anything else.
en.body_html:
A tax return is not the place for storytelling. It is the numerical account of a year of business activity. Nevertheless, certain mistakes recur every period that turn a calm document into a highly contentious one. Recognizing these mistakes is a far cheaper form of prevention than a late defense.

The first mistake is starting in the final week of the deadline. When time is short, figures are entered out of habit rather than from supporting documents. A rounded sales figure or an estimated expense may appear to complete the task, but in reality it leaves room for questions. Begin the work in the preceding weeks, even if the final bank statement has not yet arrived.

The second mistake is inconsistency between reports. The performance return, value-added tax return, seasonal transactions report, and the Taxpayers' System (Samaneh-ye Moadian) must all tell the same story. If sales appear higher in one report and lower in another, the first question is not “which software is faulty”; the real question is where the original figure came from. A simple reconciliation table prepared before submission can eliminate many risks.

The third mistake is recording expenses without supporting documents or with documents unrelated to the business activity. A fictitious invoice or a personal expense recorded under the business name may help at the time of filing but will require explanation during review. It is better to retain complete, genuine, and relevant expenses rather than decorative ones.

The fourth mistake is overlooking payroll. The insurance list, payroll tax, and wage expenses in the books must correspond with one another. Discrepancies among these three sources create questions for both the employer and the performance file.

The fifth mistake is forgetting non-routine events. Sale of assets, rental income, insurance claims, bulk discounts, or sales returns—if not reflected in the return—will later surface in account reconciliations. List these events separately.

The sixth mistake is placing complete trust in software output without reviewing the summary. Software is a tool. A human review of total sales, total purchases, and profit will reveal imported errors more quickly.

The seventh mistake is promising yourself “we’ll fix it later.” A corrective (amended) return can only be filed until the end of the legal deadline for that return (for example, end of Khordad for individuals and end of Tir for companies with a year ending in Esfand). After the deadline, corrections are no longer possible through the return and the matter goes to the tax office's audit. Even within the deadline, an amendment does not always produce a cleaner record. Treat the first submission with full seriousness.

Precision in numbers and honesty in advice—these two principles have practical meaning when preparing a tax return: do not record any figure whose source you cannot demonstrate, and do not choose a path that looks good only on paper. A calm file is one that you yourself can explain to a colleague.

en.title: Note 100 for Business Owners: Who Qualifies and What Considerations Apply?
en.description: Note 100 offers a simpler route, but it is not suitable for everyone. First assess the revenue ceiling, type of activity, and your tax record.
en.body_html:
Every year, as the tax return deadline approaches, the same phrase is heard frequently: “Note 100 is simpler; let’s go with that.” Simplicity is appealing, yet choosing simplicity without proper assessment can sometimes make next year’s file more vulnerable. Note 100 is an option, not a universal rule.

First, it must be understood that this route is primarily intended for certain business owners with specific income conditions. Legal entities are generally not the target audience. Even among sole proprietors, the type of activity, method of sales, and the revenue ceiling announced for that year are important. The income ceiling and implementation details are announced each year in the Tax Administration's instructions or notices, and last year's figure may differ this year. The deadline is the same as the self-employed income tax return: under Article 100 of the Direct Taxes Act, by the end of Khordad of the following year, with registration and payment through my.tax.gov.ir.

The second consideration is the quality of your tax history. If irregular sales were recorded in previous years, or there are discrepancies between bank transactions and declared amounts, choosing the simplified route will not necessarily eliminate those gaps. The Tax Authority may later examine other indicators. Selecting Note 100 does not end all inquiries; it merely changes the form of compliance for that year.

The third consideration is how this choice aligns with the Taxpayers' System (Samaneh-ye Moadian) and invoices. If a significant portion of sales has been recorded in the system, the figure you have in mind for Note 100 must be consistent with that data. Ignoring this alignment can make future explanations difficult.

The fourth consideration concerns the actual expenses of the business. Some taxpayers incur substantial costs and wish to reflect them in their return. In simplified routes, there is less room to display detailed expenses. If showing costs and depreciation is analytically important to you, the full route may provide greater clarity, even if it takes a little more time.

The fifth consideration is peace of mind. Some business owners simply want to close the matter for the current year and return to their core activities. If the legal conditions are met and the declared amount is not unreasonably distant from actual sales, Note 100 can deliver exactly that peace of mind. The key is that the decision must be informed, not made in a rush during the final week.

In practice, before making any recommendation we place three documents side by side: the sales picture for the year, the main cost picture, and the picture of parallel obligations such as value-added tax or seasonal transactions. When these three speak to each other, choosing between Note 100 and a full return is no longer guesswork.

Tax consulting with a long-term perspective means closing this year’s file in a way that does not force you into hasty explanations next year. Note 100 is a tool. A tool is only useful when it fits your hand.

en.title: Taxpayers' System and Electronic Invoicing: Where to Begin?
en.description: Before connecting the software, get to know the work folder, the invoice template, and the actual sales flow.
en.body_html:
For many businesses, the Taxpayers' System feels like a dark room: they know they must enter, but they do not know where the first key is. A rushed start usually leads to incorrect invoice issuance, discrepancies with the books, and end-of-period anxiety. A calmer path is to first create a clear picture of the current situation and then connect the tool.

The first step is to understand the work folder. The taxpayer must know their role in the system, whether their identity information is correctly registered, and whether branches or fixed counterparties need separate definitions. Many subsequent errors begin from this very point: an incomplete postal code, an incorrect role, or an organizational unit that exists in practice but is not visible in the system.

The second step is to understand the sales flow, not the software menu. Ask whether you sell goods or services, whether sales are cash or credit, whether the buyer is an end consumer or another taxpayer, and whether sales returns and discounts are common in your daily operations. The invoice template must match this reality. If the wrong template is chosen, subsequent corrections will take time and effort.

The third step is to standardize items and units of measure. The description of goods must match the warehouse and internal invoice. A minor difference in title or unit may seem insignificant to a human but appears as a discrepancy to the system. This is where it pays to prepare a master list of goods and services and use it as the basis for issuance.

The fourth step is the timing of issuance. An electronic invoice only makes sense if it does not have an unreasonable gap from the moment of sale. Accumulating paper invoices until the end of the month both creates the risk of penalties and makes inventory control difficult. A simple daily or at most multi-day procedure is better than a last-minute cram session.

The fifth step is to reconcile the system with accounting. If the accountant sees one report and the system shows another, the problem is not technical; it is a lack of common language. A short pilot period with a limited number of invoices, before full migration, helps identify discrepancies.

In the first consultation session, we usually pose three questions: Is the work folder healthy? Does the invoice template match the type of activity? And does the finance team know when and with what documentation they must issue? If the answer to all three is clear, connecting the software is the next step, not the first.

Tax transparency is built from these calm details. The goal is not to show speed; the goal is that at the end of each period, the sales figure in the system matches the figure in the file, and you know why it is so.

en.title: What Is an Electronic Invoice and Who Must Issue It?
en.description: What is an electronic invoice? This article explains in simple terms what these invoices are, which businesses are required to issue them, and how to get started with the Taxpayers' System (Samaneh-ye Moadian). A complete, practical guide.
en.body_html:
The electronic invoice is one of the most significant changes to Iran's tax system in recent years. If you run a business and your sales have reached a certain threshold, you are likely required to issue this type of invoice. In this article, we explain in clear, practical language what an electronic invoice is, who is obligated to issue it, and how you can meet this requirement without confusion.

What Is an Electronic Invoice?

An electronic invoice is essentially a structured, digital sales invoice. Unlike traditional paper invoices, these must be issued and transmitted through the Taxpayers' System (Samaneh-ye Moadian) of the Iranian National Tax Administration. The main objective is to increase transaction transparency, prevent tax evasion, and centralize sales data from all businesses.

Every electronic invoice has a unique identifier and is automatically recorded in the system. This identifier enables the tax authority to easily monitor the supply and sales chain.

Electronic Invoices and the Taxpayers' System (Samaneh-ye Moadian)

The Taxpayers' System (Samaneh-ye Moadian) is the platform created by the Iranian National Tax Administration for the registration and exchange of all electronic invoices. If you want to know where to begin, read our article Taxpayers' System (Samaneh-ye Moadian) and Electronic Invoices: Where Do We Start?.

There are three types of electronic invoice. Type 1 carries full seller and buyer details and is used for sales to other businesses (B2B); once the buyer confirms it in their dashboard, it creates a tax credit for the buyer. Type 2 carries full seller and goods/service details, buyer details are optional, it is typically used for sales to final consumers, and it gives the buyer no tax credit. Type 3 is the payment receipt from a card terminal (POS) or online payment gateway, which counts as an electronic invoice under the Tax Administration's rules and gives the buyer no tax credit. Source: Article 1 of the Point-of-Sale Terminals and Taxpayers' System Act, and the Tax Administration's e-invoice data specification.

Who Must Issue Electronic Invoices?

The obligation to issue electronic invoices did not start for everyone at once. The Iranian National Tax Administration has rolled it out in phases, through official "calls" (farakhan) for different groups of taxpayers. Legal entities and sole proprietors become obliged from the date announced in the call or notice that covers their group. To know your own start date, check the Administration's calls and notices and the status of your dashboard (karpusheh).

Smaller businesses may become subject to the requirement in later phases. If you are just starting out or have low turnover, it is best to review your situation with a tax consultant. For small businesses, the Simple Guide to Registering in the Taxpayers' System (Samaneh-ye Moadian) is a good starting point.

Exceptions and Special Considerations

Choosing the Note 100 method for your tax return is not, in itself, an exemption from issuing electronic invoices. When and under what conditions a business must issue e-invoices is set by the Tax Administration's calls and notices; check your status in your dashboard or with an adviser before deciding. The article Note 100 for Business Owners: Who Does It Apply To and What Are the Considerations? provides further details on this topic.

Benefits of Issuing Electronic Invoices

In addition to being a legal obligation, correct issuance of electronic invoices offers many practical advantages, including reduced human error, faster settlement with customers, easier tracking of receivables, and a lower risk of tax penalties.

Businesses that implement this system correctly from the outset will face fewer difficulties when preparing their tax returns. If you make mistakes in your tax declaration, you may receive a tax assessment notice (barg-e tashkhis). The article You Received a Tax Assessment Notice: What to Do First offers useful guidance in this regard.

How to Issue an Electronic Invoice

To issue electronic invoices, you must first register on my.tax.gov.ir and activate your Taxpayers' System (Samaneh-ye Moadian) dashboard. Then obtain a unique tax memory ID and choose how invoices are sent: directly by you, through a trusted tax service provider, or through government systems. After that, you issue and transmit invoices through connected software or directly in your dashboard.

If you encounter complexity in this process, be sure to seek assistance from a tax consultant. The team at Forough Shomar Simorgh is ready to provide specialized services in this area. To arrange a consultation, you can use our services page or consultation booking page.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is an electronic invoice and how does it differ from a regular invoice?

An electronic invoice is a structured, digital sales invoice issued and recorded through the Taxpayers' System (Samaneh-ye Moadian) and carries a unique tax identifier.

Which businesses are required to issue electronic invoices?

The obligation has been phased in: legal entities and sole proprietors must issue electronic invoices through the Taxpayers' System (Samaneh-ye Moadian) from the date announced for their group in the Tax Administration's calls or notices.

Do taxpayers under Note 100 also have to issue electronic invoices?

Choosing Note 100 is not, in itself, an exemption from electronic invoicing. Each business's obligation is set by the Tax Administration's calls and notices; check your status in your dashboard or with an adviser.

Where should we start to begin issuing electronic invoices?

First register on my.tax.gov.ir and activate your Taxpayers' System dashboard, then obtain a unique tax memory ID and choose a sending method (direct, trusted provider, or government systems). After that, issue invoices through connected software or directly in your dashboard.

Conclusion

Electronic invoicing is no longer optional; it is part of the requirements of Iran's modern tax system. The sooner you become familiar with it and implement the issuance process in your business, the less likely you are to face penalties and future problems.

Timely action, correct registration in the Taxpayers' System (Samaneh-ye Moadian), and accurate issuance of invoices are the three key factors for success in this area. If you have not yet taken action, take the first step today and seek help from specialists if needed.

en.title: VAT Return Deadline: What Happens If You Are Late?
en.description: The VAT return deadline is only 15 days after each quarter. See what late filing means and how to keep from missing the rest of the year's deadlines.
en.body_html:
Short answer

The VAT return deadline is 15 days after the end of each quarter, and an amended return is possible only until that deadline ends. Miss it, and you can no longer amend that return; the authority may, under the regulations, assess tax or impose a penalty. Take the rate from the official system or your adviser. Read the exact day for each period from the authority's notices and the compliance calendar, not from memory.

As each quarter ends, several taxpayers call to ask what happens if they file the return late. Let me be clear from the start: the VAT return deadline is short, and the window to amend that same return closes when this deadline ends. Drawing on our experience supporting small and medium-sized businesses, I will set out what this deadline means, what late filing does, and how to arrange the rest of the year's deadlines so you are not caught out. Wherever I am not certain of a rate or a circular, I will not invent a figure, and I will refer you to the official system.

How long is the VAT return deadline?

The deadline for filing the VAT return is 15 days after the end of each quarter. After spring, summer, autumn, and winter you have a short window, not a full month to put the documents in order. This is not an annual obligation; it falls four times a year, and each period stands apart from the one before.

Do not write the last day from memory. The length of Esfand, a public holiday, and sometimes a notice can change the day you need to act. For that period, check the tax compliance calendar and take the notices on the Iranian National Tax Administration information portal as your guide. If your period of activity differs from the usual pattern, check that same source with your adviser.

I often hear one mistaken view: that you can amend the return until the authority has said something. That is not the case. An amended return is possible only until the end of the legal deadline for filing that return. If you spot the error within those same 15 days, you still have time. Once the deadline ends, that door closes, and a simple amendment no longer helps.

Why does the work slip to the last days?

Card-reader reports, invoices, and the bank reconciliation are usually not ready on the first morning of the deadline. If you wait until the second week for every figure to be final, half the window is gone. In our advisory work we have made it a habit to start the close a few days before the quarter ends. We flag pending items separately and close the rest; holding the entire job does not extend the deadline.

What happens if you miss this deadline?

In late-filed cases I have almost always seen two effects, and I will not state either as a fixed percentage. The first is clear: you lose the ability to amend that return. The second is that the authority may, in accordance with the regulations, assess tax and impose a penalty for late filing or failure to file. Ask the Iranian National Tax Administration, or that quarter's adviser, for the details.

Do not treat a late return as the same thing as a tax assessment notice (barg-e tashkhis). The assessment notice is a later stage. If it is served, under Article 238 of the Direct Taxes Act you have 30 days from the date of service to attend or file an objection, after which it becomes final. Before any rushed call, read A tax assessment notice has arrived; what should you do before anything else?. Those 30 days are a live deadline too, and “I'll call next week” can mean losing the right to object.

Some people, once they are late, prefer to send nothing so they do not draw attention. That assumption is dangerous. Silence does not restore the deadline, and it usually makes the figures harder to explain. The right step is to clarify, that same week, the status of the tax file and the obligation for that period. Also see the common errors in Mistakes that make a return fragile, so a late filing is not tied to an error-filled return.

Set the year's other deadlines alongside VAT

If only VAT is on the calendar, next spring will catch you out. For business owners, the income tax return deadline and the Note 100 route both run until the end of Khordad the following year. Note 100 is not an exemption from electronic invoicing, and it is not necessarily worthwhile for every business. Before you choose, read Points to consider on Note 100 for business owners.

Legal entities have a separate calendar. Their return deadline is four months after the end of the financial year, and for a year ending in Esfand it runs until the end of Tir. Do not compare a company with a shop. Mixing up these two dates is a recurring error in files that include both an individual and a company.

Quarterly transactions under Article 169 are due 45 days after the end of the quarter. This obligation is separate from the VAT return. Missing the 15-day deadline does not cancel the 45-day obligation, or the other way around. Many calls in the third week of the following month come precisely from mixing up these two deadlines.

Electronic invoicing has no annual deadline, and the obligation has been rolled out in stages, through calls issued by the authority. Do not assume every company or every business is required to comply. If you are unsure, the tax file and the authority's notice are the guide, not your trade peers. Read the text of the laws on the National Laws and Regulations System so you do not rely on an outdated quotation.

A simple order to remember

After each quarter, VAT has 15 days and quarterly transactions have 45 days. The following year, business owners have until the end of Khordad, and companies with an Esfand year-end have until the end of Tir, for the income tax return. A tax assessment notice (barg-e tashkhis) has a separate 30-day deadline from the date of service. Put these four lines on paper; in the rush of sales, the mind swaps the dates.

A practical example from a hypothetical file

This is a hypothetical example and does not refer to any real person or shop. Suppose the owner of a home-appliance store has closed the summer with a mix of card-reader sales and several wholesale invoices. They receive the gateway report on the fifth day of the following month. On the tenth day they find that a corporate buyer was left out of total sales and that a sales return was posted twice.

If they amend by the end of the 15-day deadline, they are still within the VAT return deadline and an amendment is possible. If the work slips to the third week, that door has closed. In this hypothetical example the gap is only a few days, but the ability to amend is entirely different.

Steps in this hypothetical example

Step one: three days before the quarter ends, they close the sales and purchase lists and note pending items separately, rather than holding the whole job. Step two: in the first week of the deadline, they reconcile total sales with the card reader and the bank. Step three: they correct the omission within that same deadline by an amendment.

Step four: they keep the filing date and the tax-file status so it is later clear whether the return was actually filed or only meant to be filed. Step five: they set a separate reminder for quarterly transactions so the 45-day deadline is not mixed up with the 15-day deadline. The same sequence works for a café or a service company; the difference is the volume of documents, not the logic of the deadline.

Habits that help you not miss a deadline

From late-filed cases, a few simple habits have worked better than complex tools. Keep a single calendar; reminders scattered between a partner and the accountant mean no one is responsible. Mark each deadline three times: ten days before to gather documents, three days before to review, and the morning of the filing day.

One person should be responsible for filing, and another should only confirm that the filing actually went through. In a small business, “the accountant was supposed to send it” is heard often after the deadline, and it restores no deadline. Do not leave filing to the last night. Do not leave setting up the unique fiscal memory ID and the filing method for the deadline day either. A dropped connection, or one missing digit in the final hour, cannot be put right.

Do not issue a test invoice. That option does not exist in the main tax file, and every invoice issued is real. Curiosity about how the system reacts can create a real invoice you will later have to explain. Also check new circulars on the Iranian National Tax Administration information portal so your internal calendar does not go stale.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is it a problem if I file the VAT return one day late?

The deadline is 15 days after the end of the quarter, and when it ends you can no longer amend that return. This article does not state a fixed rate for the financial effect of one day's delay; ask the authority's system or that period's adviser.

Can I amend the VAT return after the deadline has ended?

No. An amended return is possible only until the end of the legal deadline for filing that return. After the 15-day deadline, that route is closed.

Is the VAT deadline the same as quarterly transactions?

No. The VAT return is due 15 days after the end of the quarter, and quarterly transactions under Article 169 are due 45 days after the end of the quarter. Missing one does not remove the other obligation.

How does the return deadline for business owners differ from a company's?

Business owners and Note 100 have until the end of Khordad the following year. Legal entities have four months after the end of the financial year, and for a year ending in Esfand this deadline runs until the end of Tir.

Summary

The VAT return deadline is 15 days after each quarter, and an amendment is possible only until the end of that same deadline. Put the rest of the year's deadlines on one calendar, and take the penalty rate from the official system, not from memory. If you have missed a deadline, raise it with Forough Shomar Simorgh before you act in haste; book a time on the Book a consultation page, or email info@foroughshomar.ir.

en.title: Misfiled a quarterly transaction report? Read this first
en.description: Filed the quarterly transaction report in error? Common mistakes, the difference from VAT, and how to correct them, in this practical guide.
en.body_html:
Short answer

Do not start a correction by guessing. First match that quarter against the invoices, the books, and the counterparty identifier, so you can see whether the error is in the identifier, the amount, or the type of purchase or sale. The deadline for filing the quarterly transaction report is 45 days after the end of the quarter, and you should check the correction path in the official system, because the form and the notices change. If that deadline has passed, do not leave the discrepancy unresolved: check the status on the Iranian National Tax Administration portal, or ask the adviser on that file to settle the right path before the matter reaches a tax assessment notice (barg-e tashkhis).

When you file the quarterly transaction report and then find that the buyer's identifier is off by one digit, or that an invoice amount does not agree with the books, it is natural to think of the penalty first. In our advisory work we have often seen that the main trouble does not come from the small mistake itself. It comes from the taxpayer mixing it up with the VAT return, or searching the taxpayer portal for a test invoice and issuing another real invoice instead. If you are looking only for a ready-made sentence that will delete the error, this page does not have one. The error has to be found in that same quarter, the deadline has to be taken from the official calendar, and the correction has to be made through the path the system shows that day, not from what someone remembers of a messaging-group chat.

The quarterly transaction report is not the VAT return

These two obligations look alike because both are tied to the quarter, but they do not cover the same subject. The VAT return concerns the tax and duties for that period, and the filing deadline is 15 days after the end of the quarter. The transaction list under Article 169 has a separate deadline: 45 days after the end of the quarter. If you complete both in one sitting, sales from one may be copied into the other, and you will not later know where the difference came from.

Before any correction, check the tax obligations calendar to see which deadline for that quarter is still open. Read the form and the call-up notice on the Iranian National Tax Administration information portal and the Iranian National Tax Administration. Last year's screenshot and a message in a colleagues' group are not a source for the deadline.

If sales and VAT credit still do not reconcile, close that file separately. We have set out the method in the article Quarterly VAT return: reconcile sales and credit before you file so these two obligations are not mixed in one file.

Do not take coverage from a colleague's line of work

It should not be said that every company or every business files this list. The obligation is phased and depends on the call-up notice and the type of activity. If an obligation has been opened for you in the taxpayer portal, take that as your criterion. You can see the official text of the laws on the National Laws and Regulations System, but coverage of your own file is not settled by one general sentence.

Mistakes to cross off before you file

If you cross off these patterns before filing, a large part of any later correction falls away. We have seen them often in review files, and they usually come from haste or from copying the previous quarter's file.

Counterparty identifier

The most common error is one transposed digit in the counterparty identifier. The system sometimes accepts the record, and the discrepancy surfaces later, when the other party files its own list or when matching begins. Take the identifier from the card, the contract, or an official inquiry, not from a customer message or an old letterhead. For a legal entity, do not substitute the company national ID for the manager's national ID code.

Amount, date, and type of transaction

The VAT-inclusive amount is entered instead of the amount excluding VAT, or the reverse. The invoice date falls in the first days of the next quarter but is recorded in the previous quarter. A purchase appears on a sales row because the software export swapped the column. The total of the rows must agree with the books for that quarter. If it does not, stop the filing until you find the differing line. Whether each field on the form wants the gross or the net amount, read that from the guide to the same form. We do not set a fixed template here, because the form changes.

Omissions and mix-ups with invoices

Some transactions are struck from the list because the buyer's name is not at hand. Others come in from the invoice file and are entered again by hand. A Type 1 electronic invoice carries full seller and buyer details, is used for sales to economic operators, and gives the buyer a tax credit. Type 2 makes buyer details optional, is usually a sale to the final consumer, and carries no tax credit. Type 3 is a card-reader or payment-gateway receipt and carries no tax credit. Do not treat this distinction as the same thing as the transaction-list obligation. The absence of a buyer's name is not, by itself, permission to drop the transaction.

If the scope of invoice issuance is still unclear to you, read it separately in the guide to electronic invoices and who must issue them, and only then decide what goes into this list. The obligation to issue invoices has been rolled out in phases and by call-up notice; do not assume every business is obliged today.

Another costly error is issuing an invoice in the main taxpayer portal just to test. There is no test invoice in the main taxpayer portal, and every invoice issued is real. This list is not corrected by issuing a new invoice.

A worked example: how we reconcile a hypothetical quarter

This scenario is a hypothetical example; the name and figures do not refer to a real taxpayer. Suppose a seller of office supplies notices two errors a few days after filing the spring list. In one sales row, the buyer's national ID is off by one digit. In one purchase row, the amount was taken from the card receipt, while the books show a different figure for that purchase.

Set the three columns side by side

Set three lists side by side: the books for that quarter, invoices issued and received, and the rows that actually went into the report. In this hypothetical example, only those two differences should appear. An extra difference means the statement is still incomplete, and you should not move on to a correction.

Name each error separately

The first error is an identifier error: the counterparty is the same, and only the number was entered wrong. The second is an amount error: the transaction is real, but the figure on the list does not match the figure in the books. Do not lump the two together in a general note such as a spring correction. For each line, write what was filed, what should be filed, and put the invoice number beside it. If you do not know which figure a field on the form wants, read the form guide and do not guess.

Close the correction inside that same period

If you are still within the 45 days after the end of that quarter, make the correction through the path the taxpayer portal shows for that period. After you submit, total the three columns again. Total purchases, total sales, and the number of rows must match what you intended to file. Keep the before and after versions in that quarter's folder so that, if a question comes later, you do not reconstruct the story from memory.

If, in this hypothetical example, the deadline has expired, the seller should not issue a new invoice to make up for it, invent a penalty rate, or mix the row into the next quarter so the totals appear to balance. They must check in the system whether a correction is still possible for that period, and read the latest notice on the Iranian National Tax Administration information portal. This hypothetical example is not a ruling on your file.

If the deadline has passed or the discrepancy is serious

The end of the deadline does not mean the error is wiped out, and it does not mean you may delete the row through an informal channel. First check the status of that period in the taxpayer portal and read the latest notice. If the identifier or amount discrepancy is large, act before the Administration's matching begins. Do not take a penalty figure from this page; rely only on the official source for that year.

If a tax assessment notice (barg-e tashkhis) arrives, do not count the deadline by guesswork. Under Article 238 of the Direct Taxes Act, you have 30 days from the date of service to attend or object, and after that the notice becomes final. Before writing any letter, see the first step in the guide to the first action after a tax assessment notice, so these 30 days are not used up on incomplete work.

An amended return is possible only until the end of the legal deadline for filing that same return. Do not extend this rule to the transaction list. The return deadline for business owners runs to the end of Khordad of the following year, and legal entities have four months after the end of the financial year; for a year ending in Esfand, that is the end of Tir. Do not mix these dates, in one note, with the 45-day quarterly transaction deadline and the 15-day VAT deadline.

Choosing the simplified route for the annual performance return, including where Note 100 applies, is not the answer to whether you must file the transaction list. Check each obligation separately in the taxpayer portal. Do not treat Note 100 as an exemption from electronic invoicing either.

Frequently Asked Questions

How long after the quarter ends must I file the quarterly transaction report?

The deadline for this report is 45 days after the end of the quarter. Do not confuse it with the 15-day VAT return deadline, and also check the exact day for that quarter in the obligations calendar and the Administration's notice.

I entered the buyer's identifier wrong. Should I issue a new invoice?

No. There is no test invoice in the main taxpayer portal, and every invoice issued is real. Follow up the error in that quarter's own list, through the system's correction path.

Must every business file the quarterly transaction report?

No. This obligation is not the same for every business and every company, and it depends on the call-up notice and the taxpayer's status. Check coverage in the taxpayer portal and the Administration's notices.

If the 45-day deadline has passed, can the list still be corrected?

Whether a correction is still possible after the deadline cannot be stated the same way for every file. Check the status of that period in the system and the latest notice, and if the discrepancy is material, consult the adviser on that file before a tax assessment notice (barg-e tashkhis).

Summary

Do not fix the quarterly transaction report in haste, or by issuing a new invoice. Name the error, reconcile the identifier and the amount with the books and the invoices, and keep the 45-day deadline separate from the 15-day VAT deadline. A correction only means something if the system for that period, and the latest notice, allow it.

If you have several discrepancies at once, or the period is closed and you do not know whether a correction is still open, general advice is not enough. Check that quarter's status in the system, and book a time for a file review from the consultation booking page, or email info@foroughshomar.ir.
